title: Brownian Motion Markov Properties and Hitting Times

items.title: Natural and usual augmented Brownian filtrations
items.statement: For Brownian motion B, let F_t^0=sigma(B_s:0<=s<=t) and F_infinity^0=sigma(union_t F_t^0). On the completion of the ambient probability space let N be the family of all subsets of P-null sets in F_infinity^0, put overline F_t^0=sigma(F_t^0 union N), and define the usual augmentation by F_t=intersection_{u>t} overline F_u^0. Thus F_t^0, overline F_t^0, and F_t are respectively the raw natural, completed raw, and complete right-continuous usual Brownian filtrations; F_{t+}^0=intersection_{u>t}F_u^0 denotes the uncompleted raw right limit.
items.strategy: First complete the ambient sigma-algebra and extend P in the standard unique way, so every member of N is measurable. Check that the completed raw family is increasing and complete. The intersection definition gives F_t=intersection_{v>t}F_v by cofinality of pairs u>v>t, hence right-continuity, and every F_t contains N, hence completeness. Keep the four notations F_t^0, overline F_t^0, F_{t+}^0, and F_t distinct in every later argument.
items.axiom_base: ZFC; AC is inherited from the Brownian-motion supplier

references.title: Sousi, Advanced Probability, Definition 6.10

items.title: The Brownian transition semigroup
items.statement: For bounded Borel f on R and t>=0 define P_t f(x)=E[f(x+B_t)]=integral f(y)p_t(x,y)dy, where p_t(x,y)=(2 pi t)^(-1/2)exp(-(y-x)^2/(2t)) for t>0 and P_0f=f.
items.strategy: Use the N(0,t) law of B_t and translation to obtain the kernel formula; record the t=0 convention separately.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 7.3

items.title: The Brownian kernels form a semigroup
items.statement: For s,t>=0, P_sP_t=P_{s+t}; equivalently, integral p_s(x,y)p_t(y,z)dy=p_{s+t}(x,z). Each P_t is a probability kernel operator.
items.strategy: Represent P_sP_tf(x) by independent increments B_s and B_{s+t}-B_s, apply Tonelli first to nonnegative f and positive/negative parts for bounded f, and use that their sum is N(0,s+t). This also proves the Gaussian convolution identity and mass-one property.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus: An Introduction with Applications, Section 2.6

items.title: Conditioning a known state and independent noise
items.statement: Let X be an (S,Sigma)-valued G-measurable random element and let Y be a (T,Tau)-valued random element such that sigma(Y) is independent of G, with law mu. If h:S times T->R is bounded and Sigma times Tau measurable, then H(x)=integral_T h(x,y)mu(dy) is Sigma-measurable and E[h(X,Y)|G]=H(X) almost surely.
items.strategy: Measurability of H is the published kernel-integration theorem for the constant kernel mu. For each D in G verify the conditional-expectation integral identity first when h=1_A times 1_C: the event D intersect {X in A} lies in G, so independence of sigma(Y) from G factors its intersection with {Y in C}. The product-measurable sets whose indicators satisfy every such test form a Dynkin system containing the rectangle pi-system, hence contain the product sigma-algebra. Increasing simple approximation and monotone convergence handle nonnegative h; positive and negative parts handle bounded real h. Conditional-expectation uniqueness gives the asserted almost-sure identity.
items.axiom_base: ZFC; AC is declared for conditional expectation

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 7.2.1 proof

items.title: Markov property of Brownian motion
items.statement: For deterministic s,t>=0 and bounded Borel f, E[f(B_{s+t})|F_s^0]=P_tf(B_s) almost surely. The same identity holds for the usual augmented filtration F_s.
items.strategy: For the raw filtration, finite past cylinders are independent of the increment B_{s+t}-B_s by independent increments; grouping and a monotone-class argument extend this to F_s^0. Apply the state-and-independent-noise lemma to h(x,y)=f(x+y). Completion by terminal null sets does not change this conditional identity. For t>0 choose n with 1/n<t and G_n=overline F_{s+1/n}^0. The completed-raw formula at s+1/n gives E[f(B_{s+t})|G_n]=P_{t-1/n}f(B_{s+1/n}). Levy downward convergence sends the left side in L1 to conditioning on intersection_n G_n=F_s. On the right, path continuity and L1-continuity of translated Gaussian densities give pointwise convergence to P_tf(B_s), and boundedness plus dominated convergence gives L1 convergence. Uniqueness identifies the limits. For t=0, f(B_s) is already F_s-measurable.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 7.2.1
Sousi, Advanced Probability, Definition 6.10 and the Markov argument preceding Theorem 6.13

items.title: Future-path Markov property
items.statement: For fixed s>=0, the process (B_{s+t}-B_s)_{t>=0} is a Brownian motion independent of F_s; consequently for every bounded Borel functional Phi on continuous path space, E[Phi((B_{s+t})_{t>=0})|F_s]=E_{B_s}[Phi((B_t)_{t>=0})] almost surely.
items.strategy: Replace B on its common null discontinuity event by the zero path; usual completion makes this harmless and the coordinate-generator lemma makes the resulting path maps Borel. For the raw past, independent increments give independence of every finite future-increment cylinder from every finite past cylinder; grouping and monotone class extend this to the raw past and then to bounded Borel functionals. For the usual past, first take bounded continuous future cylinders. Condition on G_n=overline F_{s+1/n}^0 with 1/n below the least positive cylinder time, split off the vanishing increment B_{s+1/n}-B_s, and use the completed-raw formula. Path continuity and dominated convergence identify the cylinder limit, while Levy downward convergence identifies conditioning on F_s. A functional monotone class and the coordinate generator extend the identity to all bounded Borel path functionals. Finally apply the state-and-independent-noise lemma to the measurable translation map (x,w)->x+w to obtain the displayed translated-Wiener kernel.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 7.2

items.title: The Brownian germ sigma-algebra at zero
items.statement: The germ sigma-algebra at zero is F_{0+}^0=intersection_{t>0}F_t^0; it records events observable arbitrarily soon after time zero.
items.strategy: Identify the uncountable intersection with the decreasing countable intersection over positive rational times by monotonicity.

references.title: Sousi, Advanced Probability, Definition 6.10 and Theorem 6.13

items.title: Blumenthal's zero-one law
items.statement: Every event A in the Brownian germ sigma-algebra F_{0+}^0 has probability zero or one.
items.strategy: The corrected future-path theorem at s=0 says that the complete future Brownian path, whose initial value is zero almost surely, is independent of the usual sigma-algebra F_0. Every A in F_{0+}^0 lies in F_0 and also lies in F_infinity^0, the sigma-algebra generated by that path. Hence A is independent of itself. Applying the product identity to A intersect A gives P(A)=P(A)^2, so P(A) is zero or one. Completion causes no gap because the future-path theorem was proved for the complete usual filtration.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 7.2.3
Sousi, Advanced Probability, Theorem 6.13

items.title: Continuous-time stopping times and stopped sigma-algebras
items.statement: For a filtration (F_t)_{t>=0}, a map tau:Omega->[0,infinity] is a stopping time when {tau<=t} is in F_t for every t. Its stopped sigma-algebra is F_tau={A:A intersect {tau<=t} is in F_t for every t}; for right-continuous filtrations the equivalent tests using {tau<t} may be used.
items.strategy: Verify that F_tau is a sigma-algebra and that a deterministic time returns F_t. From non-strict tests, {tau<t}=union_{n:1/n<t}{tau<=t-1/n}, with the t=0 event empty. Conversely, strict tests give {tau<=t}=intersection_n{tau<t+1/n}, which belongs to intersection_n F_{t+1/n}=F_t by right-continuity. Apply the same identities inside A intersections to justify the equivalent stopped-sigma-algebra tests.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 7.3

items.title: Brownian closed-set hitting times are stopping times
items.statement: If C is closed in R and tau_C=inf{t>=0:B_t in C}, then tau_C is a stopping time for both the raw natural Brownian filtration and its usual augmentation.
items.strategy: For every t>=0, continuity on the compact interval gives {tau_C<=t}=intersection_{n>=1} union_{q in Q intersect [0,t]}{dist(B_q,C)<1/n}. If the path hits C the right side is immediate by rational approximation. Conversely the right side says the continuous distance path has infimum zero on [0,t], hence attains zero and meets the closed set C. This formula is F_t^0-measurable, including t=0, so no right-continuity or initial-separation assumption is needed; the usual-filtration conclusion follows by inclusion.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 7.3.4

items.title: Strong Markov property of Brownian motion
items.statement: For every almost surely finite stopping time tau for the usual Brownian filtration, (B_{tau+t}-B_tau)_{t>=0} is a Brownian motion independent of F_tau. Equivalently the future-path conditional law given F_tau is Wiener measure translated by B_tau.
items.strategy: Approximate tau from above by tau_n=2^-n ceil(2^n tau), leaving the null event {tau=infinity} separate. Prove directly that each tau_n is a stopping time and F_tau is contained in F_{tau_n}. For a countably valued tau_n, split on {tau_n=k2^-n} in F_{k2^-n} and apply the deterministic future-path theorem, first testing against events in F_tau. Almost-sure finiteness and uniform continuity on compact sample intervals give convergence of every rational-coordinate future increment. Dominated convergence passes bounded continuous cylinder identities to tau. A monotone class in the testing events and another on continuous path space, using the coordinate generator, give independence of the entire shifted future from F_tau and the translated Wiener conditional law.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 7.3.9
Sousi, Advanced Probability, Theorem 6.17

items.title: Brownian reflection principle
items.statement: For a>0 and t>0, with M_t=sup_{0<=s<=t}B_s and tau_a=inf{s:B_s=a}, reflection after tau_a preserves Wiener law and P(M_t>=a,B_t<=b)=P(B_t>=2a-b) for b<=a. In particular P(M_t>=a)=2P(B_t>=a).
items.strategy: Do not assume tau_a is finite. For each deterministic horizon T use the bounded stopping time S=tau_a wedge T. Strong Markov at S and symmetry of an independent post-S Brownian motion show that reflection after S preserves the law on [0,T]. On {tau_a<T} this is reflection after tau_a, while on {tau_a>=T} it changes no coordinate before T. Thus every finite-horizon cylinder law of the global reflection agrees with Brownian motion; coordinate generation and continuity give equality of Wiener laws. Finally {M_t>=a}={tau_a<=t}; reflection bijects {M_t>=a,B_t<=b} with {B_t>=2a-b}, and symmetry/decomposition yield the maximum formula.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Proposition 2.7.2
Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Example 7.4.2 and equation (7.4.4)

items.title: Law of the Brownian maximum
items.statement: For t>0 and x>=0, P(M_t<=x)=2 Phi(x/sqrt(t))-1; hence M_t has the same law as |B_t| and density sqrt(2/(pi t))exp(-x^2/(2t)) on x>0.
items.strategy: Insert the centered N(0,t) tail in the reflection identity, use symmetry, and differentiate the explicit absolutely continuous distribution on (0,infinity); continuity at zero excludes an atom.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Proposition 2.7.2

items.title: Distribution of a one-sided Brownian hitting time
items.statement: For a>0 and tau_a=inf{t>=0:B_t=a}, P(tau_a<=t)=2(1-Phi(a/sqrt(t))) for t>0, and tau_a has density a(2 pi t^3)^(-1/2)exp(-a^2/(2t)) on t>0.
items.strategy: Continuity identifies {tau_a<=t} with {M_t>=a}. Substitute the maximum law and differentiate carefully by the chain rule. The CDF tends to one as t tends to infinity, so there is no mass at infinity.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, equation (7.4.6) after Example 7.4.2

items.title: One-dimensional Brownian motion hits every point almost surely
items.statement: For every fixed a in R, tau_a=inf{t>=0:B_t=a} is finite almost surely.
items.strategy: For a>0 let t tend to infinity in the hitting-time CDF. For a<0 apply symmetry to -B; a=0 is immediate from the starting convention.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 7.4

items.title: Brownian motion started at x
items.statement: For a standard d-dimensional Brownian motion B and x in R^d, the shifted process B^x=x+B is the standard d-dimensional Brownian motion started at x, and P_x denotes its law on the cylinder space; P_x is a probability measure, P_x-almost every path is continuous and starts at x, the increments have the same laws and independence as those of B, and the hitting-time functionals satisfy T_C(B^x)=T_{C-x}(B) pathwise, so P_x(T_C<=t)=P(T_{C-x}<=t) and P_x(T_b<T_a)=P(T_{b-x}<T_{a-x}).
items.strategy: Define the shifted law as the pushforward of P under the measurable map sending omega to the path t -> x+B_t, on the cylinder space. Record that the map is a random element, that continuity and increments are inherited, and that the hitting-time identity T_C(B^x)=T_{C-x}(B) holds pathwise; the scalar case d=1 and the planar case d=2 are the only instantiations used, and no kernel structure in x is claimed.
items.axiom_base: ZFC; AC is inherited from the Brownian construction

references.title: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, fifth edition, Section 7.5
Perla Sousi, Advanced Probability, Section 6.1

items.title: Two-sided Brownian exit probability
items.statement: For a<x<b and Brownian motion started at x, if tau=inf{t>=0:B_t notin (a,b)}, then tau is finite almost surely, B_tau is in {a,b}, and P_x(B_tau=b)=(x-a)/(b-a).
items.strategy: For mesh h embed the successive hitting times of the neighboring h-grid points. Strong Markov and symmetry make the stopped grid positions a simple symmetric random walk; gambler's ruin gives its upper-exit probability. Choose inner and outer lattice endpoints converging to a,b, squeeze the Brownian exit event between their grid exit events, and use path continuity. The same squeeze plus almost-sure point hitting proves finiteness; continuity forces the endpoint value.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 7.5.3

items.title: One-dimensional Brownian motion is recurrent
items.statement: Almost surely one-dimensional Brownian motion visits every nonempty open interval infinitely often; in particular it returns arbitrarily close to every point at arbitrarily large times.
items.strategy: For a fixed rational interval choose an interior rational point. After each hit, strong Markov restarts a Brownian motion, so the next hit after first reaching a different rational point is finite almost surely. Iterate countably and intersect the probability-one events. A countable rational base upgrades the assertion to all open intervals.

references.title: Sousi, Advanced Probability, Section 6.7

items.title: Planar Brownian annular exit probability
items.statement: Let W be planar Brownian motion started at x, fix y in R^2 and 0<epsilon<|x-y|<R, and put S_epsilon=inf{t>=0:|W_t-y|=epsilon}, T_R=inf{t>=0:|W_t-y|=R}, and H=S_epsilon wedge T_R. Then H is finite almost surely and P_x(S_epsilon<T_R)=log(R/|x-y|)/log(R/epsilon).
items.strategy: The rational-distance formula for a continuous adapted path makes H a stopping time. One coordinate almost surely reaches a level forcing |W-y|>=R, so continuity makes H finite. Construct a bounded C^2 radial function phi by explicit quintic Hermite splices, equal to log|z-y| on the closed annulus and constant near y and outside a larger ball. Independent vector increments plus the state-and-noise lemma, Fubini, dominated convergence, and two finite-interval integrations by parts in the planar Gaussian kernel prove Q_h phi-phi=(1/2) integral_0^h Q_r Delta phi dr; conditioning the same identity proves that phi(W_t)-phi(W_0)-(1/2)integral_0^t Delta phi(W_r)dr is a martingale. Before H the Laplacian term is zero. Approximate H wedge n from above by dyadic stopping times for the sampled martingale and apply the published discrete optional-sampling theorem. As the dyadic mesh vanishes, path continuity handles phi and the bounded Laplacian makes the post-H integral remainder vanish; dominated convergence then sends n to infinity. The stopped logarithm is bounded between log epsilon and log R, and continuity puts W_H on one boundary. Thus log|x-y|=P(S_epsilon<T_R)log epsilon+P(T_R<S_epsilon)log R; the two boundary events partition because H is finite, and solving gives the formula.
items.axiom_base: ZFC; AC is inherited from Brownian motion and optional sampling, and Countable Choice and Dependent Choice are explicit at Lebesgue integration by parts

references.title: Sousi, Advanced Probability, Section 6.7, annular logarithm calculation, printed pp. 63-64

items.title: Raw versus usual filtrations in strong Markov
items.statement: The strong Markov theorem above is stated for the completed right-continuous usual augmentation. The raw natural filtration is sufficient at deterministic times but need not be right-continuous and is not silently substituted at stopping times.
items.strategy: Trace the dyadic approximation proof: inclusion F_tau subset F_{tau_n} and passage from strict to non-strict stopping events use the usual hypotheses. Point forward only to the companion counterexample for the strictness phenomenon, not as a premise.

references.title: Sousi, Advanced Probability, Sections 6.3-6.5

title: Brownian Motion Markov Properties and Hitting Times — Examples

items.title: Brownian density and Gaussian convolution
items.statement: For s,t>0, direct completion of the square evaluates integral_R p_s(x,y)p_t(y,z)dy as p_{s+t}(x,z), illustrating the Brownian semigroup.
items.strategy: Multiply the two Gaussian densities, complete the square in y, extract the N(m,st/(s+t)) normalizing integral, and simplify the remaining exponent and constant.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Section 2.6

items.title: Maximum crossing before a fixed time
items.statement: For a>0 and T>0, P(sup_{0<=s<=T}B_s>=a)=2(1-Phi(a/sqrt(T))); numerical or symbolic threshold calculations therefore reduce to one standard-normal tail.
items.strategy: Identify the crossing event with the maximum tail and substitute the scaled normal CDF; check the limits a down to zero and a up to infinity.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 7.4

items.title: A Brownian hitting time has infinite mean
items.statement: For a>0, tau_a has density a(2 pi t^3)^(-1/2)e^{-a^2/(2t)} and E tau_a=infinity.
items.strategy: Use the proved density. For t>=a^2 the exponential factor is bounded below by e^{-1/2}; hence the first-moment integrand is bounded below by a positive multiple of t^{-1/2}, whose integral diverges. This avoids an invalid differentiation or optional-stopping argument.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Section 2.7

items.title: Exit side from an interval
items.statement: Brownian motion started at x in (-2,3) exits at 3 with probability (x+2)/5 and at -2 with probability (3-x)/5; at x=0 these are 2/5 and 3/5.
items.strategy: Substitute a=-2 and b=3 in the two-sided exit formula, take the complement for the lower endpoint, and verify the probabilities sum to one.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 7.5.3

items.title: Successive hits restart independent Brownian copies
items.statement: Starting at 0, define T_0=0 and T_{n+1}=inf{t>T_n:|B_t-B_{T_n}|=1}. Then the path segments (B_{T_n+t}-B_{T_n})_{0<=t<=T_{n+1}-T_n} are independent and identically distributed stopped Brownian excursions to {-1,1}, and all T_n are finite almost surely.
items.strategy: Inductively show T_n is a stopping time by shifting the closed-set hitting-time construction. At T_n, strong Markov makes the shifted future an independent Brownian motion; its first hit of {-1,1} is finite. Iterate conditional factorization for bounded segment functionals to obtain mutual independence and equality of laws.

references.title: Sousi, Advanced Probability, Sections 6.5-6.7

items.title: Planar coordinate hitting does not imply point hitting
items.statement: For planar Brownian motion W=(B^1,B^2), each coordinate hits every prescribed real value almost surely, and every nonempty disc is visited almost surely, yet every prescribed point of R^2 is polar: P_x(tau_y<infinity)=0 for x!=y.
items.strategy: Coordinate recurrence is the one-dimensional theorem applied separately and does not synchronize the two coordinate hitting times. Fix y and an outer radius R>|x-y|. Hitting y before leaving the outer disc implies hitting every epsilon-circle first, so the annular formula and epsilon down to zero give probability zero. A path that ever hits y is bounded before its finite hitting time, hence hits y before T_R for some integer R; a countable union proves polarity. For a nonempty disc, if x is outside choose an epsilon-ball inside it. The annular formula with fixed epsilon tends to one as R tends to infinity, so that ball, hence the disc, is hit almost surely; if x is already inside there is nothing to prove.

references.title: Sousi, Advanced Probability, Section 6.7, printed pp. 63-64

items.title: The raw natural Brownian filtration need not be right-continuous
items.statement: On canonical Wiener space, the raw natural filtration satisfies F_0^0 strictly contained in F_{0+}^0: there is a nonempty null germ event absent from F_0^0.
items.strategy: Let A be the set of continuous paths that vanish throughout [0,1/m] for some m. It is nonempty. Continuity makes each fixed-m condition a countable intersection over rational coordinates, so for every t>0 a sufficiently large m shows A is in F_t^0. Its probability is zero because even B_{1/m}=0 has probability zero. But F_0^0=sigma(B_0)={empty,Omega}, so A is not in F_0^0.

references.title: Sousi, Advanced Probability, Definition 6.10

items.title: Strong Markov fails at a nonstopping random time
items.statement: Let L=sup{s<=1:B_s=0}. Then L is not a stopping time and the post-L process is not an independent Brownian motion: on (L,1] it has a constant nonzero sign.
items.strategy: Continuity and recurrence ensure L is well defined and L<1 almost surely because P(B_1=0)=0. By definition there is no zero in (L,1], so continuity fixes the sign there. A fresh Brownian motion has zeros arbitrarily close to zero: the event of an immediate one-sided sign has germ probability zero by Blumenthal plus symmetry. Hence the post-L future cannot have the strong-Markov law. If L were a stopping time, the strong Markov theorem would give that law, a contradiction.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Sections 7.3-7.5

items.title: Almost-sure finiteness does not imply integrability
items.statement: The first time tau_1 at which standard Brownian motion hits 1 satisfies P(tau_1<infinity)=1 but E tau_1=infinity.
items.strategy: The first dependency proves almost-sure finiteness and the second computes the divergent expectation. Explicitly distinguish a finite-valued random variable almost surely from an L1 random variable.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Section 2.7

items.title: Brownian paths are nowhere locally one-half Hölder
items.statement: Almost surely, on no nondegenerate interval I does there exist a finite C with |B_t-B_s|<=C|t-s|^(1/2) for every s,t in I.
items.strategy: Fix a rational interval [a,b] and integer C. If the bound holds, then for every equal n-partition all n standardized increments have absolute value at most C. Independence makes this event have probability p_C^n with p_C<1, hence the intersection over n has probability zero. A countable union over rational subintervals and integer ceilings for C covers every proposed local one-half-Hölder interval; no uncountable union is taken.

references.title: Yoshida, Probability Theory, Section 6.3
Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 7.1

items.title: Brownian paths are nowhere differentiable
items.statement: Almost surely, a one-dimensional Brownian path has no finite derivative at any time t>=0 (with right derivative at t=0).
items.strategy: Use the Dvoretsky-Erdos-Kakutani mesh argument. If a path is differentiable at some s in a compact rational interval, then for some integer C and all fine meshes, the three consecutive mesh increments surrounding s are each at most 5C/n. For a fixed mesh location these are independent N(0,1/n) variables, so the probability is at most (K C/sqrt(n))^3; union over O(n) locations is O(C^3/sqrt(n))->0. Take the increasing union over locality scales, then count over C and rational compact intervals. The endpoint uses one-sided increments.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 7.1.6

items.title: Brownian paths have infinite total variation
items.statement: Almost surely, the total variation of a Brownian path on every nondegenerate compact interval is infinite.
items.strategy: On a fixed rational interval use its dyadic partition and S_n=sum|Delta B|. Direct Gaussian integration gives E|N(0,h)|=sqrt(2h/pi); independence gives E S_n proportional to 2^(n/2) and Var(S_n) bounded uniformly. Chebyshev makes P(S_n<=half E S_n)=O(2^-n), so Borel-Cantelli implies S_n tends to infinity. Total variation dominates S_n. Intersect over countably many rational intervals, each contained in every nondegenerate interval. This direct proof deliberately avoids the defective published BV-differentiability prerequisite.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Section 2.8

items.title: Quadratic variation along a partition sequence
items.statement: For continuous x on [0,T] and partitions pi_n with mesh tending to zero, define [x]^{pi_n}_t=sum_{[u,v] in pi_n, v<=t}(x_v-x_u)^2, optionally adding (x_t-x_u)^2 on the unique interval containing t. Quadratic variation along (pi_n) is a limit of these processes in the stated pointwise or uniform mode; no partition-independent claim is built into the definition.
items.strategy: State both step and partial-increment conventions and show their difference is bounded by the largest squared oscillation on a mesh interval, hence vanishes for each continuous path when mesh tends to zero.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Section 2.8

items.title: Brownian quadratic variation on dyadic partitions
items.statement: For fixed T>0 and dyadic partitions of [0,T], sum_k(B_{(k+1)T/2^n}-B_{kT/2^n})^2 converges to T in L2 and almost surely.
items.strategy: Each increment has variance h=T/2^n, fourth moment 3h^2, and independent squares. Thus the sum has expectation T and variance 2T^2/2^n, proving L2 convergence. Chebyshev gives a summable error probability for each epsilon; apply Borel-Cantelli to epsilon=1/m and intersect over m to obtain almost-sure convergence.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Theorems 2.8.1-2.8.2

items.title: Uniform dyadic Brownian quadratic variation process
items.statement: For fixed T>0, the dyadic partial quadratic-variation processes [B]^n_t converge almost surely uniformly in t in [0,T] to t, for either the step or partial-increment convention.
items.strategy: At dyadic grid points write [B]^n_{kT/2^n}-kT/2^n as partial sums of independent centered variables (Delta B)^2-h. Kolmogorov's maximal inequality bounds the probability of a grid maximum exceeding epsilon by 2T^2/(2^n epsilon^2), summable in n; Borel-Cantelli and rational epsilon give uniform grid convergence. Between grid points the time error is at most h, and the two process conventions differ by at most the maximum squared Brownian oscillation over a mesh interval, which tends to zero by uniform continuity of each continuous sample path.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Section 2.8

items.title: Brownian one- and quadratic variation
items.statement: Almost surely Brownian paths have infinite total (one-)variation on every nondegenerate interval, while along every fixed dyadic time mesh their quadratic variation on [0,t] equals t simultaneously for 0<=t<=T.
items.strategy: Intersect the probability-one events from the two supplied results over integer horizons T. The first conclusion is intrinsic; explicitly retain the dyadic-partition qualifier on the second.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Section 2.8

items.title: Brownian motion has a jointly measurable continuous version
items.statement: Every standard Brownian motion B has an indistinguishable version B-hat such that every path t->B-hat_t(omega) is continuous, omega->B-hat(omega) is Borel measurable into C([0,infinity),R) with its uniform-on-compacts topology, and (t,omega)->B-hat_t(omega) is jointly measurable.
items.strategy: Intersect the single measurable probability-one continuity event in the Brownian definition with {B_0=0}, and replace the whole path by the zero path on its complement. The resulting version is indistinguishable, starts at zero, and has every path continuous. Each time coordinate remains measurable; since path-space Borel sets are generated by coordinates, omega->B-hat(omega) is a Borel random element. Prove evaluation C times [0,infinity)->R is continuous for the uoc topology: near (f,t), uniform control on one compact interval containing t and continuity of f control |g(s)-f(t)|. Joint measurability is then the composition of the measurable path map times the identity with continuous evaluation.
items.axiom_base: ZFC; AC is inherited from Brownian motion

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Section 7.1, Brownian path normalization; combined with the published continuous-path coordinate-generator dependency

items.title: The Brownian zero set
items.statement: Fix the all-path continuous jointly measurable version B-hat. Its zero set is Z={t>=0:B-hat_t=0}; on a horizon T write Z_T=Z intersect [0,T]. Indistinguishability makes all almost-sure assertions obtained from this normalization assertions about the original Brownian motion.
items.strategy: Every normalized path is continuous, so Z is closed, and the normalization makes 0 belong to Z for every outcome. Joint measurability ensures the indicator 1_{B-hat_t=0} is product-measurable for later Tonelli arguments.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, unnumbered zero-set discussion in Section 7.4.1

items.title: The Brownian zero set has Lebesgue measure zero
items.statement: For every T<infinity, the Lebesgue measure of Z_T is zero almost surely.
items.strategy: Tonelli gives E lambda(Z_T)=integral_0^T P(B_t=0)dt. For every t>0 the N(0,t) density has no atom, while t=0 is a Lebesgue-null singleton. The nonnegative random variable lambda(Z_T) therefore has expectation zero and so vanishes almost surely; intersect over integer T.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, unnumbered zero-set calculation in Section 7.4.1

items.title: The Brownian zero set has no isolated points
items.statement: Almost surely every t in Z is a limit point of other zeros; equivalently Z is perfect as a closed subset of [0,infinity).
items.strategy: Blumenthal plus symmetry shows Brownian motion starting at zero takes both signs arbitrarily soon, hence has zeros arbitrarily soon by continuity. For every rational q, let tau_q be the first zero after q; recurrence makes it finite, it is a stopping time, and strong Markov transfers the immediate-return property to tau_q. On the intersection of these countably many probability-one events, any zero t is approached from the right if t=tau_q for some q<t, or from the left by tau_q as rational q increases to t. Closedness comes from continuity.

references.title: Sousi, Advanced Probability, Theorem 6.39, printed p. 71
Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, unnumbered zero-set discussion in Section 7.4.1

items.title: The Brownian zero set is uncountable
items.statement: Almost surely the Brownian zero set is uncountable in every interval [0,T] with T>0.
items.strategy: Fix a positive rational q. Almost surely B_q is nonzero, while immediate return at zero supplies nonzero-time zeros before q. Hence Z_q is nonempty and closed, and the global no-isolated-points theorem leaves no isolated point in Z_q: zero is approached from the right, every zero below q has nearby zeros still below q, and q itself is absent. Apply the perfect-set uncountability theorem. Intersect over rational q; for arbitrary T>0 choose rational q<T and use Z_q subset Z_T.

references.title: Sousi, Advanced Probability, Theorem 6.39, printed p. 71

items.title: Two-sided Mills bounds for the standard normal tail
items.statement: Let phi(x)=(2 pi)^(-1/2)exp(-x^2/2) and barPhi(x)=integral_x^infinity phi(y)dy. For every x>0, x phi(x)/(1+x^2)<=barPhi(x)<=phi(x)/x. In particular, for x>1, (x^(-1)-x^(-3))phi(x)<=barPhi(x)<=x^(-1)phi(x).
items.strategy: For y>=x, 1<=y/x and phi'(y)=-y phi(y), giving the upper bound after integration. On each [x,R], the C^1-to-AC theorem and the Lebesgue integration-by-parts theorem give integral_x^R phi=phi(x)/x-phi(R)/R-integral_x^R phi(y)/y^2 dy. Let R tend to infinity by monotone convergence and the elementary Gaussian boundary limit. Bounding the residual integral by x^(-2)barPhi(x) and rearranging gives the stronger lower bound x phi(x)/(1+x^2); elementary algebra implies the displayed x^(-1)-x^(-3) form.
items.axiom_base: ZFC; Countable Choice and Dependent Choice are explicitly declared for Lebesgue integration by parts

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Gaussian tail estimates in the proof of Theorem 8.5.1

items.title: Brownian law of the iterated logarithm at infinity
items.statement: Almost surely limsup_{t->infinity} B_t/sqrt(2t log log t)=1 and liminf_{t->infinity} B_t/sqrt(2t log log t)=-1, with the expression taken for t>e.
items.strategy: For the upper bound, reflection and the upper Mills estimate make P(sup_{s<=c^n}B_s>(1+eta)sqrt(2c^n log n))=O(n^{-(1+eta)^2}/sqrt(log n)), hence summable. First Borel-Cantelli and interpolation on [c^{n-1},c^n], followed by rational c down to one and eta down to zero, give limsup<=1; apply the same argument to -B for an eventual absolute upper bound. For the lower bound fix epsilon>0, choose c so large that there is a with a^2/(1-1/c)<1 and a-(1+eta)c^(-1/2)>1-epsilon. The independent block increments B_{c^n}-B_{c^{n-1}} have variance c^n(1-1/c); the lower Mills bound makes the probabilities of exceeding a sqrt(2c^n log n) divergent. Second Borel-Cantelli gives infinitely many such blocks, and the absolute upper bound at c^{n-1} converts them to B_{c^n}>(1-epsilon)sqrt(2c^n log n). Countable rational epsilon gives limsup>=1; symmetry gives liminf=-1. Replacing log n by log log(c^n) changes the normalization by a factor tending to one.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 8.5.1

items.title: Brownian law of the iterated logarithm at zero
items.statement: Almost surely limsup_{t downarrow 0} B_t/sqrt(2t log log(1/t))=1 and the corresponding liminf is -1.
items.strategy: For t>0 set W_t=tB_{1/t}; time inversion says W is Brownian. Substitute s=1/t in the infinity LIL for W and simplify t W_{1/t}=B_t and the normalizing factor. Symmetry supplies the lower limit.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 8.5.1, combined with Brownian time inversion

items.title: The critical Hölder boundary at zero
items.statement: Almost surely Brownian motion is locally alpha-Hölder for every alpha<1/2, but is not one-half-Hölder at zero; indeed |B_t|/sqrt(t) is unbounded as t down to zero.
items.strategy: The published Kolmogorov-continuity consequence gives every subcritical exponent (intersect over rational alpha and weaken exponents). The zero-time LIL gives subsequences with |B_t|/sqrt(t) asymptotic to sqrt(2 log log(1/t)), which diverges, contradicting any critical Hölder constant.

references.title: Yoshida, Probability Theory, Section 6.3, subcritical Holder regularity and the critical-boundary remark
Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 8.5.1

items.title: Quadratic variation needs a partition convention
items.statement: The identity [B]_t=t proved here is an almost-sure assertion for the fixed dyadic sequence (and comparable preselected regular sequences), not a simultaneous assertion over all path-dependent or arbitrary refining partitions. Without restrictions, quadratic variation can depend on the chosen partitions.
items.strategy: Separate the quantifiers: the probability-one set is selected after fixing a partition sequence. Explain that adapting partitions to a realized oscillatory path invalidates the independence estimates and can alter sums; do not claim a universal pathwise quadratic variation theorem.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Section 2.8

items.title: The last Brownian zero has the arcsine law
items.statement: For fixed t>0 let L_t=sup{s<=t:B_s=0}. Then for 0<=u<=t, P(L_t<=u)=(2/pi)arcsin(sqrt(u/t)); equivalently L_t/t has density 1/(pi sqrt(x(1-x))) on (0,1).
items.strategy: Condition at deterministic u. Given B_u=x, no zero occurs in (u,t] exactly when a Brownian motion started at x avoids zero for t-u; reflection identifies this probability as 2Phi(|x|/sqrt(t-u))-1. Integrate against the N(0,u) density, use symmetry, and evaluate the resulting planar Gaussian wedge probability (or differentiate under the integral and integrate from zero) to obtain (2/pi)arcsin sqrt(u/t). Differentiate on (0,t) and check endpoint masses vanish.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Example 7.4.3 and equation (7.4.7)

items.title: Brownian step-potential resolvent at zero
items.statement: For alpha,beta>0 let V(x)=alpha+beta 1_{x>0} and u(x)=E_x integral_0^infinity exp(-integral_0^t V(B_s)ds)dt, using the jointly measurable continuous Brownian version. Then 0<=u<=1/alpha, u is C^1 on R and C^2 off zero, satisfies u''/2=alpha u-1 on x<0 and u''/2=(alpha+beta)u-1 on x>0, and u(0)=1/sqrt(alpha(alpha+beta)).
items.strategy: Joint measurability, kernel-integration measurability, and Tonelli make u a bounded Borel function with 0<=u<=1/alpha. Write G_alpha f(x)=integral_0^infinity e^{-alpha t}P_tf(x)dt. The pathwise identity e^{-alpha t}-e^{-integral_0^t V(B_r)dr}=integral_0^t e^{-alpha s}(V(B_s)-alpha)e^{-integral_s^t V(B_r)dr}ds, followed by Tonelli and the corrected future-path Markov property, gives u=G_alpha 1-G_alpha(beta 1_{(0,infinity)}u). Evaluate the Gaussian time integral by a scalar change of variables and the Gaussian integral to obtain G_alpha f(x)=(1/sqrt(2alpha))integral_R exp(-sqrt(2alpha)|x-y|)f(y)dy. Splitting at y=x and using dominated convergence shows this convolution is C^1 for bounded Borel f; where f is continuous, elementary differentiation gives (G_alpha f)''/2=alpha G_alpha f-f. Consequently u is C^1, is C^2 on each open half-line, and obeys the stated ODEs. Boundedness forces u(x)=1/alpha+A exp(sqrt(2alpha)x) for x<0 and u(x)=1/(alpha+beta)+C exp(-sqrt(2(alpha+beta))x) for x>0. Continuity of u and u' at zero gives sqrt(alpha)(u(0)-1/alpha)=-sqrt(alpha+beta)(u(0)-1/(alpha+beta)); solving yields u(0)=1/sqrt(alpha(alpha+beta)).
items.axiom_base: ZFC; AC is inherited from Brownian conditional laws

references.title: Yoshida, Probability Theory, Lemmas 6.8.1-6.8.3, printed pp. 214-216

items.title: Brownian positive occupation time has the arcsine law
items.statement: For t>0, A_t=integral_0^t 1_{B_s>0}ds satisfies P(A_t/t<=x)=(2/pi)arcsin(sqrt(x)) for 0<=x<=1; its density is 1/(pi sqrt(x(1-x))).
items.strategy: Joint measurability defines A_t and Tonelli identifies the resolvent lemma's value u(0) with integral_0^infinity e^{-alpha t}E[e^{-beta A_t}]dt. Brownian scaling gives A_t equal in law to tA_1, so another Tonelli calculation makes this transform E[(alpha+beta A_1)^(-1)]=1/sqrt(alpha(alpha+beta)). The probability density pi^{-1}[x(1-x)]^{-1/2} integrates to one under x=sin^2(theta), and the same substitution followed by z=tan(theta) evaluates its transform as 1/sqrt(alpha(alpha+beta)). For uniqueness fix alpha=1 and |beta|<1: the geometric series for (1+beta x)^(-1) converges uniformly on [0,1], so equality of the transforms for positive beta near zero equates every moment. Real Stone-Weierstrass makes polynomials uniformly dense in C[0,1], hence the two probability laws agree on continuous functions and therefore agree. Rescaling from A_1 to A_t proves the stated CDF and density.

references.title: Yoshida, Probability Theory, Proposition 6.8.4, printed pp. 216-217

items.title: Expected dyadic quadratic variation
items.statement: For the 2^n equal subintervals of [0,T], E sum_k(Delta_k B)^2=T exactly for every n.
items.strategy: Each increment is N(0,T/2^n), so its second moment is T/2^n. Sum the 2^n expectations; independence is not needed for this mean calculation.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Section 2.8

items.title: Variance of dyadic quadratic variation
items.statement: For the same sum Q_n, Var(Q_n)=2T^2/2^n, so Q_n converges to T in L2.
items.strategy: For X~N(0,h), E X^4=3h^2, hence Var(X^2)=2h^2. Independent increments have independent squares, so variances add: 2^n times 2(T/2^n)^2 is 2T^2/2^n. Mean-square convergence follows.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Theorem 2.8.1

items.title: A null uncountable random closed set
items.statement: Almost surely, for every T>0 the Brownian zero set Z intersect [0,T] is closed and uncountable but has Lebesgue measure zero.
items.strategy: Intersect the probability-one events from the nullity and uncountability results over positive rational horizons. Continuity supplies closedness. Emphasize that uncountability does not imply positive Lebesgue measure.

references.title: Sousi, Advanced Probability, Theorem 6.39, printed p. 71

items.title: The Brownian p-variation threshold
items.statement: Almost surely on every nondegenerate compact interval, Brownian paths have finite p-variation for every p>2 and infinite p-variation for every 1<=p<=2.
items.strategy: For p>2 choose alpha with 1/p<alpha<1/2; the local Holder bound gives a uniform finite bound on every partition sum. For 1<=p<2, finite p-variation would bound each dyadic quadratic sum by (max|Delta B|)^(2-p)V_p, which tends to zero by continuity, contradicting dyadic quadratic variation T. For p=2, finite strong two-variation would make its accumulated variation v(t) finite and monotone with |B_{t+h}-B_t|^2<=v(t+h)-v(t). The published monotone differentiability theorem makes the right quotient of v finite for almost every t. Stationary increments and the zero-time LIL give limsup_{h down to0}|B_{t+h}-B_t|^2/h=infinity almost surely at each deterministic t; Fubini upgrades this to almost every t on almost every path, a contradiction. Prove the claims first on rational compact intervals and rational p in the planned ranges; countable intersection and monotonicity of p-variation for bounded paths extend them to every real p>2 and every real 1<=p<=2.
items.axiom_base: ZFC; AC is inherited from Brownian motion, and Countable Choice is separately declared at the monotone-differentiability use

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Section 2.8, quadratic variation
Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 8.5.1, Brownian LIL

items.title: LIL rules out a square-root-time bound
items.statement: Almost surely there is no finite random C and delta>0 such that |B_t|<=C sqrt(t) for all 0<t<delta.
items.strategy: The zero-time LIL supplies a sequence t_n down to zero for which |B_{t_n}|/sqrt(t_n) is asymptotic to sqrt(2 log log(1/t_n)), which diverges. This contradicts every finite C.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Theorem 8.5.1

items.title: Continuity does not imply finite quadratic variation
items.statement: There is a continuous function x on [0,1] and refining partitions with mesh tending to zero for which the quadratic sums diverge to infinity.
items.strategy: For m>=1, on I_m=[2^{-(m+1)},2^{-m}] draw a piecewise-linear sawtooth with N_m=m^4 teeth, alternating between 0 and a_m=1/m and ending at 0; put x=0 on {0} union [1/2,1]. The endpoint values and a_m->0 make x continuous. Let pi_n be the union of the dyadic grid {k2^{-n}:0<=k<=2^n} and every sawtooth vertex in blocks I_1,...,I_n. These finite partitions are nested and have mesh at most 2^{-n}. No dyadic-grid point lies inside I_n, while its sawtooth vertices all belong to pi_n, so block I_n alone contributes exactly 2N_na_n^2=2n^2. Hence the quadratic sums tend to infinity along the refining sequence.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Section 2.8 (partition-dependence warning)

items.title: Finite quadratic variation does not imply finite total variation
items.statement: Almost every Brownian path has dyadic quadratic variation [B]_t=t but infinite total variation on every nondegenerate interval, so finite quadratic variation along the specified meshes does not imply bounded variation.
items.strategy: Choose any path in the probability-one intersection supplied by the dependency. On that deterministic continuous path, the dyadic quadratic sums are finite and converge to elapsed time while the supremum of absolute-increment sums is infinite.

references.title: Lawler, Stochastic Calculus, Section 2.8

items.title: Fixed-time assertions do not yield a pathwise nowhere statement
items.statement: There is a continuous random process X on [0,1] such that for every fixed deterministic t the path is almost surely not differentiable at t, while almost surely the path is differentiable somewhere; hence the fixed-time assertion does not upgrade to a pathwise nowhere-differentiability statement.
items.strategy: On ([0,1],Lebesgue) with the uniform coordinate omega, put G(s):=s^2 T(s) for the Takagi function T and X_t(omega):=G(|t-omega|). G is continuous, differentiable at 0 with derivative 0, and nowhere else differentiable because T=G/s^2 would then be differentiable there. Each path is therefore differentiable exactly at t=omega and non-differentiable at every t in (0,1) with t different from omega; for each fixed t the exceptional set {omega=t} is a Lebesgue null singleton, while almost surely the path is differentiable at its own shift, exhibiting the invalid uncountable interchange of quantifiers that a fixed-time Brownian argument would make.

references.title: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, discussion before Theorem 7.1.6
